title: Victorinus (8.2)
hookLine: a well-known old orator makes his profession of faith in public
tomorrow: what could a monk in the desert teach a professor?

lines: A NAME, SAID BACK BY A CROWD.
cards: Senior night. They read a name over the speakers, and the whole gym says it back, a sound you can feel in your chest.
Augustine hears about a sound like that from Simplicianus, an older man in Milan whom Bishop Ambrose loved like a father.

The story is about Victorinus, an aged, learned teacher of speech in Rome, so honored that the city put up his statue in the Forum. When he finally stood up in church to say the creed, the crowd whispered his name.
Why would a man like that risk it?

teach.b: First, the private faith. Victorinus had been reading scripture on his own, and he'd tell Simplicianus quietly: you should know I'm already a Christian.
Simplicianus answered: I won't believe it until I see you in the church. Victorinus laughed. In Augustine's Latin: ergo parietes faciunt christianos?
So do walls make Christians? Second, the fear.
Augustine says what held him back was fear of offending his proud friends. Then, by reading, he grew more afraid of something else: of being denied before the angels, as the Gospel warns.

In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Whosoever shall confess me before men, him shall the Son of man also confess before the angels of God." One day he simply said: let's go to the church. Third, the choice.
In Rome, people about to be baptized said the creed from a raised place, in front of everyone. The priests offered Victorinus a private profession instead.
He chose the public one. Fourth, the sound.
As he went up, people who knew him whispered his name to one another, then went quiet to hear him, and he spoke the faith with confidence.
One to tell a friend tonight: the answer to do walls make Christians turned out to be a voice, out loud, in a full room.

how: Adults entering the Catholic Church make a public profession of faith, often at the Easter Vigil, after a time of preparation; at Sunday Mass the congregation says the Creed aloud together.

o: a bishop who baptized Augustine in Milan
an emperor who built the churches of Rome
an old teacher who said his faith in public

p: I won't believe it until I see you in church
where the creed was said aloud
whispered his name, then went quiet

s: Victorinus started believing the day he walked into church
he'd been reading and believing privately; the church was where he said it aloud.
do walls make Christians? was Victorinus's own joke
he said it to Simplicianus, more than once, laughing.
the priests insisted Victorinus speak in public
they offered him a private profession. he chose the public one.

games.q: your cousin is getting confirmed and asks if she can skip saying anything aloud and just sign the form. what does the Victorinus story offer her?
o: saying it out loud can be the step that makes it hers.
the form is enough, since walls don't make Christians.
only well-known people need to say their faith out loud.
games.why: Victorinus already believed in private. He was offered a quiet way, and chose to say it in front of everyone.

practice: Choose one line you hold, or one you're still learning: a line of the Creed, a verse, one true sentence about your life. Say it aloud, just loud enough to hear your own voice, and listen to how it sounds outside your head.
Then let the sit hold the quiet after it.

wordCard.voice: Victorinus. The well-known old teacher of Rome who could have said his faith in private, and chose to say it in public.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 8.2: so do walls make Christians? Victorinus's joke to Simplicianus.

carryVoice: In public: some things only become yours when you say them out loud, where people can hear. Until tomorrow.
